title: A Code Written in a Thousand Genes
paragraphs: The eye solves an enormous problem with a small kit: three kinds of cone cell, each tuned to a different band of wavelengths, let a person tell apart millions of colors.
The ear sorts sound by frequency along a single membrane in the inner ear.
Smell offers no such shortcut: odor molecules come in tens of thousands of shapes, and there is no single property, nothing like wavelength or pitch, along which they can be lined up.
How the nose makes sense of that crowd was, until 1991, one of the largest open questions in sensory biology.
The olfactory epithelium is a patch of tissue high in the nasal cavity, and in a human it holds millions of olfactory sensory neurons.

Each is a slender bipolar cell: a tuft of cilia at one end sits in the mucus lining the nose, and a thin axon at the other climbs through the cribriform plate, a perforated sheet of bone, into the olfactory bulb.
These neurons are unusual in that they die and are replaced throughout life, each lasting weeks to months before a new one grows from a stem cell below.

By the late 1980s researchers had shown that odorants raise the level of cyclic AMP in the cilia, and in 1989 Randall Reed's group at Johns Hopkins identified a G protein, named G-olf, concentrated in olfactory neurons.
Both findings pointed toward a known class of proteins, the G protein-coupled receptors, which cross the cell membrane seven times and hand their signal to a G protein inside the cell.
Linda Buck, then a postdoctoral researcher in Richard Axel's laboratory at Columbia University, built her search on three assumptions.

The receptors would be G protein-coupled receptors; they would be made in the olfactory epithelium and nowhere else; and because odorants are so varied, they would form a large family of related genes rather than one gene with a broad appetite.
She used the polymerase chain reaction with deliberately loose primers, matched to stretches shared by known receptors of the class, so that unknown relatives would be copied too.
The decisive trick was to look not for one new gene but for amplified fragments that turned out to be mixtures of many closely related sequences, exactly what a large family would produce.

Buck and Axel published the result in the journal Cell in 1991, and in 2004 they shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery and for the picture of the olfactory system that grew from it.
The family turned out to be vast.
Mice and rats carry roughly 1,000 functional odorant receptor genes, a few percent of all their genes, which makes this the largest gene family in the mammalian genome.
Humans carry a smaller working set, roughly 400, alongside hundreds of pseudogenes, copies that have accumulated mutations and are no longer translated into working receptors.
It is tempting to read those counts as a ranking of noses, rat at the top and human far below, but I think the gene tally is a crude yardstick, for reasons I will return to.
A second discovery gave the family its logic.
Each olfactory sensory neuron expresses only one of the thousand or so receptor genes, and it uses only one of its two copies of that gene, the maternal or the paternal.
The choice looks random within broad zones of the epithelium, and once a neuron has settled on a receptor, a feedback signal from the receptor protein itself appears to lock out the alternatives.
Every neuron is therefore a specialist, and the brain can read its identity from the receptor it carries.
That identity is preserved in the wiring.

Neurons expressing the same receptor are scattered across the epithelium, yet their axons gather at the same small knots of nerve endings in the bulb, called glomeruli, typically two per bulb out of roughly 2,000 in a mouse.
In 1996 Peter Mombaerts and colleagues in Axel's laboratory made the convergence visible by attaching a marker gene to one receptor gene in mice and following the stained axons to their glomerulus.

Two years later the same laboratory swapped one receptor's coding sequence for another's and saw the axons change destination, evidence that the receptor protein steers the axon as well as detecting odorants.
The bulb is therefore a map, though a map of receptors rather than of space: a given smell becomes a particular pattern of active glomeruli.
The deepest question remained: with hundreds of receptor types and far more odorants, how is identity encoded?

In 1999 Buck's own laboratory, by then at Harvard Medical School, answered it by recording from individual mouse neurons as odorants washed over them, then fishing out the receptor gene each responsive neuron carried.
Three rules emerged.
A single receptor recognizes several odorants; a single odorant is recognized by several receptors; and different odorants are recognized by different combinations of receptors.
The scheme is a combinatorial code, the olfactory equivalent of spelling words from a fixed alphabet, and with hundreds of letters the number of possible words is beyond counting.

The same study found that a small change to a molecule, such as lengthening its carbon chain by one unit, changes which receptors respond, and that raising the concentration of an odorant recruits additional receptors.
That last finding is a plausible explanation for an old puzzle: indole, which smells of flowers when dilute, smells of decay when concentrated.
How many smells can such a code distinguish?
For most of the twentieth century the standard answer was about 10,000, a figure that rested on very little evidence.

In 2014 a group at Rockefeller University asked volunteers to pick the odd one out among mixtures drawn from 128 odorants and extrapolated from their success to an estimate of more than one trillion distinguishable stimuli.
Soon afterward other researchers showed that the extrapolation was extremely sensitive to its assumptions and that modest changes in method moved the estimate by many orders of magnitude.
I find neither number persuasive as a number.
What the episode did establish is more modest and more durable: people can tell apart mixtures that differ in only a fraction of their components, which is not the mark of a weak sense.
That brings me back to the gene count.

The belief that humans smell poorly is older than the gene family; it goes back at least to the nineteenth-century anatomist Paul Broca, who noted that the human olfactory bulb is small relative to the rest of the brain and classed our species among the weak smellers.
In 2017 the neuroscientist John McGann of Rutgers University reviewed the evidence and argued that this reputation is a myth.

Counted by the neurons it contains rather than by its share of the brain, the human bulb is not unusual among mammals, and in direct tests humans are more sensitive than dogs and rodents to some odorants, though less to others.

The 400 working genes, in other words, support a far better instrument than the tally suggests; I suspect that what differs most between species is not the nose but what each animal does with the information.
One more feature is often invoked.
From the glomeruli, the bulb's output cells send their axons directly to the olfactory cortex, and from there the signal reaches the amygdala and the hippocampus, regions tied to emotion and memory.
Every other major sense passes through the thalamus before reaching its cortex; smell, on its main path, does not.

This anatomy is often offered as the reason a smell can summon a childhood kitchen so abruptly, and it may be right, but I would hold it loosely: the directness of a pathway and the vividness of a memory are not the same kind of fact.
What Buck and Axel found, in the end, was not a receptor for each smell but a way of doing without one.
A thousand genes, one per neuron, wired to a map of glomeruli and read as combinations, let a finite set of detectors cover an open-ended world of molecules.
That is a different kind of answer from the eye's three cones, and a more generous one: the nose did not need to know in advance which molecules would exist.

questions.stem: According to the passage, smell differs from vision and hearing in that
choices: it relies on far more sensory neurons than either of the other two senses
its stimuli are processed in the inner ear rather than in the brain
it depends on three kinds of receptor cell rather than on one
its stimuli cannot be ordered along a single physical property
it was the only sense whose receptors were understood before 1991

proof.quote: there is no single property, nothing like wavelength or pitch, along which they can be lined up

questions.why: Paragraph 1 lines up the three senses: the eye uses wavelength, the ear uses frequency, and for smell there is no single property along which odor molecules can be lined up. That missing axis is the difference.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: paragraph 2 gives a count for olfactory neurons but never compares it with the other senses.
Wrong sense: paragraph 1 places the membrane in the inner ear for hearing, and smell is handled in the olfactory bulb and cortex.
Reversed: the three cone types belong to the eye, and paragraph 1 presents them as the shortcut smell lacks.
Reversed: paragraph 1 says the question of how the nose works was still open until 1991.

questions.stem: According to the passage, olfactory sensory neurons are unusual among neurons because they
choices: send their axons through the thalamus before reaching the olfactory cortex
are replaced throughout life as older cells die off and new ones grow
carry cilia that reach into the mucus lining the nose
cross a bone on their way from the nose to the brain
hand their signal to a G protein inside the cell

proof.quote: These neurons are unusual in that they die and are replaced throughout life

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says these neurons are unusual in that they die and are replaced throughout life, with a new one growing from a stem cell beneath. Only that feature is labeled unusual.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 10 says smell is the sense that does not pass through the thalamus on its main path.
True but answers a different question: paragraph 2 describes the cilia without calling them unusual.
True but answers a different question: the cribriform plate is part of the route, not the feature the passage calls unusual.
Wrong level: paragraph 2 says this about G protein-coupled receptors in general, not about what makes these neurons unusual.

questions.stem: The author mentions cyclic AMP and the G protein G-olf in paragraph 2 primarily to
choices: show that the chemistry of smell was fully understood before 1991
contrast the human olfactory system with the rat's
explain how a single neuron chooses one receptor gene from the family
introduce the molecule that each odorant must bind before it is sensed
show what evidence pointed to the kind of protein Buck would seek

proof.quote: Both findings pointed toward a known class of proteins, the G protein-coupled receptors
The receptors would be G protein-coupled receptors

questions.why: Paragraph 2 closes by saying both findings pointed toward the G protein-coupled receptors, and paragraph 3 opens with Buck assuming exactly that class. The two details are there to set up her first assumption.
distractorNotes: Too strong: paragraph 1 says how the nose works was still an open question until 1991.
Outside the passage: paragraph 2 does not compare species.
Wrong paragraph: the one-receptor-per-neuron rule is paragraph 5, and it is not explained by cyclic AMP.
Wrong molecule: an odorant binds its receptor; cyclic AMP is a signal made inside the cell afterward.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 3, the word 'appetite' most nearly means
choices: a craving for food that grows with time
the range of molecules a receptor accepts
the amount of energy a cell consumes
a receptor's speed in handing its signal to a G protein
a researcher's eagerness to find a gene

proof.quote: a large family of related genes rather than one gene with a broad appetite

questions.why: Paragraph 3 contrasts a large family of genes with one gene with a broad appetite, so the appetite is how many different odorants a single receptor would have to take in. The everyday meaning, hunger, does not fit a gene.
distractorNotes: This is the common meaning of the word, and it is wrong here: a gene does not crave food.
Nothing in the sentence concerns energy use; the contrast is about how many odorants one receptor would handle.
Speed is not at issue in the sentence, which is about breadth of recognition.
The sentence describes a hypothetical gene, not a researcher's feelings.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the decisive step in Buck's search was
choices: looking for amplified fragments that were mixtures of related sequences
designing primers that matched one receptor gene and no other
sequencing the complete genome of the rat to count receptor genes
comparing the olfactory epithelium with tissue from the olfactory bulb
attaching a marker gene to a receptor gene so its product could be traced

proof.quote: The decisive trick was to look not for one new gene but for amplified fragments that turned out to be mixtures of many closely related sequences

questions.why: Paragraph 3 names the decisive trick directly: looking for amplified fragments that were mixtures of many closely related sequences, which is what a large family would produce.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 3 says the primers were deliberately loose so that unknown relatives would be copied too.
Outside the passage: no genome sequencing is described.
Outside the passage: the search was in olfactory tissue; no comparison with the bulb is mentioned.
Wrong paragraph: the marker gene experiment is Mombaerts' work in paragraph 6, five years later.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the pseudogenes in the human odorant receptor family
choices: are expressed in the olfactory epithelium and nowhere else
outnumber the functional receptor genes of mice and rats
descend from copies that once encoded working receptors
were first described by Buck and Axel in 1991
are the reason humans smell poorly compared with rats

proof.quote: copies that have accumulated mutations and are no longer translated into working receptors

questions.why: Paragraph 4 defines pseudogenes as copies that have accumulated mutations and are no longer translated into working receptors. No longer means they once were, so each pseudogene descends from a copy that used to work.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: the location of expression is an assumption about the receptors in paragraph 3, and pseudogenes are not translated at all.
Contradicted: paragraph 4 puts human pseudogenes in the hundreds and rodent functional genes at roughly 1,000.
Outside the passage: the 1991 paper is credited with finding the family, and nothing ties it to pseudogenes.
Contradicted: paragraphs 4 and 9 argue that the gene tally is a crude yardstick and that the poor-smell reputation is a myth.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a single olfactory sensory neuron
choices: expresses both the maternal and the paternal copy of one receptor gene
expresses a receptor chosen for it by the glomerulus its axon reaches
switches to a new receptor gene whenever one is locked out
expresses several receptor genes drawn from one zone of the epithelium
uses just one receptor gene and only one of that gene's two copies

proof.quote: expresses only one of the thousand or so receptor genes, and it uses only one of its two copies of that gene

questions.why: Paragraph 5 states the rule in one line: each neuron expresses only one receptor gene, and only one of its two copies of that gene, the maternal or the paternal.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 5 says only one of the two copies is used.
Reversed: paragraph 6 says the receptor helps steer the axon to its glomerulus, not the other way around.
Contradicted: paragraph 5 says that once a neuron settles on a receptor, the alternatives are locked out.
Contradicted: the zone is where the choice is made, and the neuron expresses one gene, not several.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the number of glomeruli in a mouse olfactory bulb is best explained by
choices: each receptor type being assigned about two glomeruli
each odorant being assigned a glomerulus of its own
each neuron sending its axon to a separate glomerulus
each zone of the epithelium having its own glomerulus
each glomerulus holding axons from several receptor types

proof.quote: typically two per bulb out of roughly 2,000 in a mouse
Mice and rats carry roughly 1,000 functional odorant receptor genes

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says the axons for one receptor gather at typically two glomeruli per bulb, out of roughly 2,000, and paragraph 4 gives roughly 1,000 receptor genes in a mouse. Two glomeruli for each of 1,000 receptors is about 2,000.
distractorNotes: Wrong unit: paragraph 6 says the bulb is a map of receptors rather than of odorants, and odorants far outnumber glomeruli.
Contradicted: millions of neurons converge on about 2,000 glomeruli, so many axons share each one.
Wrong paragraph: zones in paragraph 5 are where the receptor choice is made, not units of the bulb.
Reversed: paragraph 6 says axons from the same receptor gather together, which ties a glomerulus to one receptor type.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the 1999 study from Buck's laboratory found all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: A single receptor can recognize several different odorants.
Raising an odorant's concentration recruits additional receptors.
A small change in a molecule's structure changes which receptors respond.
Odorants that smell alike share most of the receptors they activate.
Different odorants are recognized by different combinations of receptors.

proof.quote: A single receptor recognizes several odorants
raising the concentration of an odorant recruits additional receptors
a small change to a molecule, such as lengthening its carbon chain by one unit, changes which receptors respond
different odorants are recognized by different combinations of receptors

questions.why: Paragraph 7 lists the three rules and then two more findings about structure and concentration. Nothing in the passage links similar smells to shared receptors; that statement cannot be confirmed anywhere.
distractorNotes: Stated in paragraph 7 as the first of the three rules.
Stated in paragraph 7 as the finding that explains the indole puzzle.
Stated in paragraph 7, with the carbon chain as the example.
Stated in paragraph 7 as the third of the three rules.

questions.stem: The author mentions indole in paragraph 7 primarily to
choices: show that a single receptor can recognize several chemically unrelated odorants
prove that the 1999 study's findings apply to humans as well as mice
suggest how recruiting more receptors could alter a smell's character
give an example of an odorant whose receptor has not been identified
illustrate how lengthening a carbon chain alters a molecule's smell

proof.quote: That last finding is a plausible explanation for an old puzzle
raising the concentration of an odorant recruits additional receptors

questions.why: Paragraph 7 introduces indole right after the finding that raising concentration recruits additional receptors, calling it a plausible explanation for an old puzzle. Indole is the illustration of what a changing receptor set might do to a smell.
distractorNotes: Wrong rule: one receptor recognizing several odorants is a separate finding, and indole is a single odorant.
Too strong and outside: the author calls the link plausible, not proven, and says nothing about human subjects here.
Outside the passage: nothing is said about which receptors respond to indole.
Wrong example: the carbon chain illustrates structural change; indole illustrates concentration.

questions.stem: Which new situation best illustrates the combinatorial code described in paragraph 7?
choices: A panel of ten lamps whose lit-and-unlit pattern names any one of hundreds of rooms
A hotel that gives every guest a key that opens that guest's room and no other room
A smoke alarm that sounds the same tone no matter what kind of smoke reaches it
A thermometer whose single reading climbs steadily as the temperature of a room rises
A phone directory in which each name appears beside one number assigned to it alone

proof.quote: different odorants are recognized by different combinations of receptors
the olfactory equivalent of spelling words from a fixed alphabet

questions.why: Paragraph 7's rule is that identity is carried by the combination of detectors that respond, like spelling words from a fixed alphabet. A small set of lamps whose on-and-off pattern names hundreds of rooms is the same idea: few detectors, many combinations.
distractorNotes: One key for one room is a one-to-one code, the opposite of the passage's scheme, in which each receptor serves several odorants.
A single detector with a broad response, but no combination of detectors to read.
A single graded signal, not a pattern across many detectors.
One-to-one pairing again: each name has its own number, so nothing is read in combination.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the 2014 study at Rockefeller University
choices: tested 128 volunteers on their ability to name single odorants
confirmed the long-standing estimate of about 10,000 smells
was accepted without objection by other researchers
showed that humans are more sensitive than dogs to certain odorants
extrapolated from an odd-one-out task to over a trillion stimuli

proof.quote: asked volunteers to pick the odd one out among mixtures drawn from 128 odorants and extrapolated from their success to an estimate of more than one trillion distinguishable stimuli

questions.why: Paragraph 8 describes the study: volunteers picked the odd one out among mixtures, and the researchers extrapolated from that success to more than one trillion distinguishable stimuli.
distractorNotes: Number swap: 128 is the count of odorants, not volunteers, and the task was comparing mixtures, not naming.
Reversed: the trillion estimate replaced the old figure of about 10,000.
Contradicted: paragraph 8 says other researchers soon showed the extrapolation was extremely sensitive to its assumptions.
Wrong paragraph: the comparison with dogs is McGann's point in paragraph 9.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the published estimates of how many smells people can distinguish is best described as
choices: admiring
skeptical
indifferent
hostile
amused

proof.quote: I find neither number persuasive as a number.
a figure that rested on very little evidence

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says the old figure rested on very little evidence and then, of both numbers, I find neither persuasive as a number. Doubting both while crediting what the work did establish is a skeptic's stance.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the author doubts both figures rather than praising them.
Too weak: the author takes a clear position and then says what the episode did establish.
Too strong: the author grants that the study established something modest and durable.
Wrong register: nothing in paragraph 8 is playful.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Paul Broca judged human smell to be weak on the basis of
choices: the small number of functional receptor genes in humans
the number of neurons in the human olfactory bulb
head-to-head tests of humans against dogs and rodents
the olfactory bulb's small size relative to the brain
the absence of a relay through the thalamus

proof.quote: who noted that the human olfactory bulb is small relative to the rest of the brain and classed our species among the weak smellers

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says Broca noted that the human olfactory bulb is small relative to the rest of the brain and on that basis classed our species among the weak smellers.
distractorNotes: Anachronism: Broca worked in the nineteenth century, and the gene family was found in 1991.
Reversed: counting neurons is the measure McGann used to answer Broca.
Wrong source: the direct tests are part of McGann's case in paragraph 9, not Broca's.
Wrong paragraph: the thalamus appears in paragraph 10 and is never tied to Broca.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a rat, with roughly 1,000 working receptor genes, compared with a human, who has about 400,
choices: can detect every odorant at a lower concentration
has an olfactory bulb that holds more than twice as many neurons
does not necessarily possess the more capable sense of smell
distinguishes roughly two and a half times as many distinct smells
uses a larger share of its glomeruli for each odorant

proof.quote: I think the gene tally is a crude yardstick
humans are more sensitive than dogs and rodents to some odorants, though less to others

questions.why: Paragraph 4 calls the gene tally a crude yardstick for ranking noses, and paragraph 9 reports that humans beat rodents on some odorants and lose on others. Put together, the larger gene count does not settle which nose is better.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 9 says humans are more sensitive to some odorants.
Outside the passage: paragraph 9 says bulb neuron counts are not unusual across mammals, and never ties them to gene counts.
Outside the passage: no such arithmetic appears, and the author rejects simple counts.
Outside the passage: nothing links the number of receptor genes to how many glomeruli an odorant uses.

questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following is true of the olfactory bulb EXCEPT:
choices: Its signals relay through the thalamus before reaching cortex.
Its output cells send axons directly to the olfactory cortex.
In the mouse it contains roughly 2,000 glomeruli.
Broca noted that in humans it is small relative to the rest of the brain.
Counted by neurons, the human bulb is not unusual among mammals.

proof.quote: send their axons directly to the olfactory cortex
roughly 2,000 in a mouse
the human olfactory bulb is small relative to the rest of the brain
the human bulb is not unusual among mammals
smell, on its main path, does not

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says every other major sense passes through the thalamus, and smell, on its main path, does not. The other four statements appear in paragraphs 6, 9 and 10.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 10, sentence 2 says the output cells send their axons directly to the olfactory cortex.
Paragraph 6, sentence 2 gives roughly 2,000 glomeruli in a mouse bulb.
Paragraph 9, sentence 2 reports Broca's observation about the bulb's relative size.
Paragraph 9, sentence 4 says the human bulb, counted by neurons, is not unusual among mammals.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Humans can distinguish more than a trillion smells, far more than scientists believed for most of the twentieth century
The sense of smell is poorly developed in humans because so many of their odorant receptor genes have become pseudogenes
A large family of receptor genes, one per neuron and read in combination, lets the nose identify countless molecules
Buck and Axel's method of loose primers and mixed fragments remains the standard way to find new gene families
The olfactory bulb's direct connection to the amygdala and hippocampus explains why smells trigger vivid memories

proof.quote: How the nose makes sense of that crowd
The scheme is a combinatorial code
let a finite set of detectors cover an open-ended world of molecules

questions.why: Paragraph 1 poses the question of how the nose handles a crowd of molecules, paragraph 7 names the combinatorial code, and paragraph 11 sums it up: a finite set of detectors covers an open-ended world. The gene family, the one-per-neuron rule and the code are the spine of the passage.
distractorNotes: One disputed estimate from paragraph 8, and the author does not find it persuasive.
Reversed: paragraph 9 argues that the poor-smell reputation is a myth.
Too narrow and outside: the method is one paragraph, and the passage never calls it a standard.
One detail from paragraph 10, and one the author says to hold loosely.
